evidence.claim: An old turnpike connects Guilford’s green with the road to Durham.
evidence.quote: The road from Guilford center to Durham center was chartered as a private turnpike in 1824, known as the Guilford and Durham Turnpike.

evidence.claim: Route 77 leads from Guilford’s town green through North Guilford into Durham, with state scenic designation along its entire length.
evidence.quote: Route 77 is a state highway in southern Connecticut. It is a state-designated scenic road and runs from the Guilford town green, through North Guilford, into the town center of Durham.

evidence.claim: The drive passes Lake Quonnipaug on the way inland.
evidence.quote: becoming the main road through the northern part of Guilford, past Lake Quonnipaug.

evidence.claim: A separate 1.4-mile scenic section of Route 17 continues through Durham, from Route 77 to just north of Route 68.
evidence.quote: A 1.4-mile (2.3 km) section in Durham, from the junction with Route 77 to just north of the junction with Route 68, is a designated state scenic road.

evidence.claim: Guilford’s green is framed by churches and civic buildings; Durham’s western side is flanked by the traprock heights of the Metacomet Ridge.
evidence.quote: Town Green: 7.7 acres in the town's historic district, surrounded by shops, churches, the town hall

evidence.claim: Guilford’s green is framed by churches and civic buildings; Durham’s western side is flanked by the traprock heights of the Metacomet Ridge.
evidence.quote: The west side of Durham is flanked by the Metacomet Ridge, a mountainous trap rock ridgeline

evidence.claim: In 1824, the road between the two town centers was chartered as the private Guilford and Durham Turnpike.
evidence.quote: The road from Guilford center to Durham center was chartered as a private turnpike in 1824, known as the Guilford and Durham Turnpike.

evidence.claim: Connecticut took over its main through roads in 1922, incorporating the old alignment into State Highway 112.
evidence.quote: In 1922, Connecticut took over the maintenance of the main through routes and State Highway 112 was established, incorporating the old turnpike alignment from Guilford to Durham

evidence.claim: In 1932, the portion south of Durham center became Route 77.
evidence.quote: In the 1932 state highway renumbering, Route 77 was created from the portion of old Highway 112 south of Durham center.

evidence.claim: Its original southern end was US 1; the extension to Route 146 followed in 1962.
evidence.quote: The original Route 77 ended at US 1. It was extended south to Route 146 in 1962.

evidence.claim: Start on Whitfield Street at the green, follow its west side, then leave on Church Street.
evidence.quote: Route 77 begins at an intersection with Route 146 at the Guilford town green as Whitfield Street. It runs around the west side of the green, then shifts to Church Street as it leaves the green.

evidence.claim: Beyond US 1 and I-95, the road becomes Durham Road.
evidence.quote: Route 77 crosses US 1 and I-95 (at exit 58), becoming the main road through the northern part of Guilford, past Lake Quonnipaug. Between I-95 and the Durham town line, Route 77 is known as Durham Road.

evidence.claim: The Route 80 junction provides connections toward Killingworth and North Branford before the road crosses into Durham.
evidence.quote: It has a junction with Route 80 (leading to Killingworth and North Branford)

evidence.claim: Across the Durham town line it becomes Guilford Road and ends at Route 17 just south of the center.
evidence.quote: then crosses into the town of Durham, where the road changes name to Guilford Road. Route 77 runs for another 2.3 miles (3.7 km) in Durham and ends at an intersection with Route 17 just south of the town center

evidence.claim: At Guilford’s green, Route 77 follows the west side before leaving on Church Street.
evidence.quote: It runs around the west side of the green, then shifts to Church Street as it leaves the green.

evidence.claim: The green occupies 7.7 acres in Guilford’s historic district, with churches, shops and the town hall along its edges.
evidence.quote: Town Green: 7.7 acres in the town's historic district, surrounded by shops, churches, the town hall

evidence.claim: Nearby on Union Street, the Sabbathday House preserves a shelter for churchgoing families.
evidence.quote: The Sabbathday House is located in a residential setting a short way northeast of Guilford's town green, on the south side of Union Street

evidence.claim: Colonial churchgoers attended morning and afternoon Sunday services. Families traveling long distances needed somewhere to rest between them.
evidence.quote: In colonial Guilford as in other communities, churchgoers attended both morning and afternoon services on Sundays.  Families that traveled long distances to attend needed a place to rest in between these services.

evidence.claim: The town allocated land for these shelters, and as many as thirty were built. This house is one of two that survive in Guilford.
evidence.quote: The town allocated several parcels in near the church for this purpose, and as many as thirty small houses were built for this purpose.  This one was probably built in 1735 by Daniel Bowen, and is one of two Sabbathday houses to survive in the town.

evidence.claim: The house’s roof combines a gambrel front with a rear shed roof, above wooden clapboards and an irregular pair of front windows.
evidence.quote: it is a 1+1⁄2-story wood-frame structure, finished in wooden clapboards and covered by a roof that is gambreled in the front and a shed roof in the rear.  The front facade is relatively plain, with a pair of sash windows irregularly placed.

evidence.claim: Route 77 passes Lake Quonnipaug in northern Guilford.
evidence.quote: becoming the main road through the northern part of Guilford, past Lake Quonnipaug.

evidence.claim: Guilford’s largest lake has a 41-acre park with a pavilion, picnic tables and a supervised beach.
evidence.quote: Lake Quonnipaug: Allowing access to the largest lake in Guilford, this property includes a 41-acre park with bathrooms, picnic tables, a pavilion, and a supervised beach.

evidence.claim: Durham’s Main Street follows a ridge between swampy areas, a layout that limited the street grid.
evidence.quote: Main Street was laid out along a ridge of high land between swampy areas that were a defining feature of the town at the time.  The swampiness prevented the formation of a full grid of streets

evidence.claim: The agricultural town’s center benefited from travelers between Hartford and New Haven, with taverns and other services along their route.
evidence.quote: The town was primarily agricultural, but the center benefited from being on a major route between Hartford and New Haven, with taverns and other services for travelers.

evidence.claim: Shoemaking developed as a cottage industry in the early nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: In the early 19th century, shoemaking arose as a cottage industry

evidence.claim: Its civic buildings changed use, too: the town hall occupies a Greek Revival church built in 1849. The historic district also includes a library built in 1901.
evidence.quote: Non-residential buildings include the town hall, a Greek Revival church built in 1849 that has been converted to that use, as well as the 1901 library

evidence.claim: The district’s houses span Federal and Victorian styles and include simpler buildings constructed for mill workers, alongside the more elaborate residences.
evidence.quote: The residential architecture includes a few examples of high-style architecture, ranging from the Federal to the Victorian, but also includes examples of vernacular buildings constructed for lower-class mill workers.
